content: Eczema, also known as atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition that significantly impacts patients' quality of life. It cannot currently be prevented or cured. Topical anti-inflammatory treatments are commonly used to manage symptoms, but there is uncertainty regarding the relative efficacy and safety of these treatments. A network meta-analysis was conducted to compare and rank the effectiveness and safety of various topical anti-inflammatory therapies for eczema. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving individuals of all ages with eczema of any severity. However, trials focusing on clinically infected eczema, seborrhoeic eczema, contact eczema, or hand eczema were excluded. Treatments were required to be used for at least one week and compared against another anti-inflammatory treatment, no treatment, or a vehicle/placebo. Trials involving topical antibiotics used alone, complementary therapies, emollients used alone, phototherapy, wet wraps, or systemic treatments were excluded. The primary outcomes assessed were patient-reported eczema symptoms, clinician-reported eczema signs, and investigator global assessment (IGA). Secondary outcomes included health-related quality of life, long-term control of eczema, withdrawal from treatment or study, and local adverse effects such as application-site reactions, pigmentation changes, and skin thinning/atrophy. Confidence in the evidence was quantified using the CINeMA framework. A total of 291 studies involving 45,846 participants were included, with most studies conducted in high-income countries and in secondary care settings. The majority of participants were adults, with only 31 studies focusing on children under 12 years of age. Most studies included both male and female participants and multiple ethnic groups, though predominantly white populations were represented. The median treatment duration was 21 days, and trial participation lasted a median of 28 days, ranging from 7 days to 5 years. The interventions studied included topical corticosteroids (TCS), topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCI), phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibitors, Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, aryl hydrocarbon receptor activators, and other topical agents. Comparators included vehicles or other anti-inflammatory treatments. A high risk of bias was identified in 89% of the trials due to issues such as selective reporting. For patient-reported symptoms, tacrolimus 0.1%, potent TCS, and ruxolitinib 1.5% were ranked as the most effective treatments, though the confidence in these findings was low. Mild TCS, roflumilast 0.15%, and crisaborole 2% were among the least effective. Sensitivity analyses indicated that potent/very potent TCS had similar effectiveness to potent TCI and were more effective than mild TCI and PDE-4 inhibitors. For clinician-reported signs, potent TCS, tacrolimus 0.1%, ruxolitinib 1.5%, and delgocitinib 0.5% were ranked as the most effective treatments, with moderate confidence. Mild TCS, roflumilast 0.15%, crisaborole 2%, and tapinarof 1% were the least effective. Class-level analyses showed that potent/very potent TCS were more effective than potent TCI, mild TCI, JAK inhibitors, and PDE-4 inhibitors. In terms of investigator global assessment (IGA), ruxolitinib 1.5%, delgocitinib 0.5%, delgocitinib 0.25%, very potent TCS, potent TCS, and tacrolimus 0.1% were ranked as the most effective treatments, with moderate confidence. Mild TCS, crisaborole 2%, pimecrolimus 1%, roflumilast 0.15%, difamilast 0.3% and 1%, and tacrolimus 0.03% were among the least effective. Longer-term outcomes over 6 to 12 months suggested a possible increase in effectiveness for pimecrolimus 1% compared to vehicle and greater treatment success with mild/moderate TCS compared to pimecrolimus 1%. Regarding local adverse effects, tacrolimus 0.1%, crisaborole 2%, tacrolimus 0.03%, and pimecrolimus 1% were most likely to cause application-site reactions. Very potent, potent, moderate, and mild TCS were least likely to cause such reactions. There was no evidence of increased pigmentation changes with TCS or crisaborole 2%. Short-term use of TCS (median 3 weeks) did not show evidence of increased skin thinning, but longer-term use (6 to 60 months) was associated with increased skin thinning compared to TCI. In conclusion, potent TCS, JAK inhibitors, and tacrolimus 0.1% were consistently ranked among the most effective treatments for eczema, while PDE-4 inhibitors were among the least effective. Mild TCS and tapinarof 1% were also ranked as less effective. TCI and crisaborole 2% were most likely to cause local application-site reactions, while TCS were least likely. Short-term use of TCS did not increase the risk of skin thinning, but longer-term use did.
